Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
This communication is in response to application No. 18/411,853 Electric Drive Unit with a Secondary Oil Reservoir; filed on 01/12/2024. Claims 1 - 20 are currently pending and have been examined. Claims 1 - 20 have been rejected as follows,
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis (i.e., changing from AIA  to pre-AIA ) for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.

Claims 1-8, 10-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Onishi (JP 2014 119084 A) in view of Bodary (US 11,440,348 B1).
Regarding Claim 1, Onishi discloses;
a differential assembly (differential apparatus 1; Fig. 1) that includes a ring gear (ring gear 7; Fig. 5) that interfaces with a gear (pinion gear 8), such that an input shaft drives rotation of the ring gear; (paragraph 33 describes the pinion gear as driven by the drive shaft and meshing with the ring gear.)
a housing, comprising: a housing body (differential carrier 2; Fig. 5);
a housing cover (cover 4) that cooperates with the housing body to define an interior region (gear accommodation chamber 3; Fig. 5) of the housing in which the differential assembly is disposed, wherein the interior region includes a primary oil reservoir (Fig. 5 and paragraph 40 describe the lubricating oil (OL) being stored in the lower part of the gear accommodating chamber.);

a gasket (gasket 10) coupled with the housing cover such that the housing cover and the gasket cooperate to define a secondary oil reservoir (lubricating oil reservoir 18; Fig. 5), the gasket defining an opening (opening 15) and at least one passage (drain hole 16; Fig. 5, paragraph 37), wherein rotation of the ring gear is configured to deliver oil into the secondary oil reservoir from the primary oil reservoir via the opening defined by the gasket, and the at least one passage is configured to convey oil to a portion of the differential assembly. (paragraphs 35-37 describe the gasket and oil flow through the opening and the drain holes.)
Onishi does not disclose an electric drive unit, a transmission assembly or that the housing body also contains the transmission assembly. However Bodary teaches;
An electric drive unit, comprising: a motor that drives rotation of a rotor shaft; (Column 2, lines 11-25 of Bodary describe the axle assembly as being attached to a torque source such as an electric motor or an internal combustion engine. See also Fig. 2)
a transmission assembly operably coupled with the rotor shaft; (Column 3, line 60 to column 5, line 7 of Bodary describe the drop gear set 26 and clutch collar 28 as transmitting power from input shaft 24 to the differential unit at pinion 32. See also Fig. 2)
a transmission assembly, such that a gear (drive pinion 32) of the transmission assembly interfaces with a ring gear (ring gear 180; Fig. 2) of the differential assembly such that rotation of the rotor shaft drives rotation of the ring gear. (Column 5, Lines 8-36 of Bodary describe the differential assembly (34) as receiving torque from the drive pinion (32) via the ring gear (180).)
a housing in which the transmission assembly and differential assembly are disposed, (differential  housing 62, axle housing 60, cover 84; Fig. 2)
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include an electric drive unit comprising a motor that drives rotation of a rotor shaft, a transmission assembly, and a housing which contains the transmission along with the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to vehicle drive systems. As disclosed by Bodary, it is well known for a vehicle drive system to consist of an electric drive comprising a motor that drives a rotor shaft, a transmission assembly, and a housing which contains the transmission along with the differential assembly. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include an electric drive comprising a motor that drives rotation of a rotor shaft, a transmission assembly, and a housing which contains the transmission along with the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as such a modification would provide the ability to utilize an electric motor as a motive power source for a vehicle.
Regarding Claim 2, Onishi does not disclose, at least one elongated tubular conduit, however Bodary teaches;
wherein at least one elongated tubular conduit (conduits 52, 54; Figs. 3, 4, Column 9, lines 11-22) that defines the at least one passage, the at least one elongated tubular conduit extending outward from the secondary oil reservoir (lubricant reservoir 50, consisting of tanks 220 and 222. Fig. 3, 4).
(Onishi creates a secondary oil reservoir within the cover utilizing a gasket with holes to control the return flow of the lubricant. Bodary teaches an auxiliary lubricant reservoir with conduits to direct returning lubricant to specific bearings. Adding the flow directing conduits of Bodary to the lubricating oil reservoir (created by the gasket, within the cover) of Onishi would provide the conduits as part of the gasket.)
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include an elongated tubular conduits that define a passage as taught by Bodary, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to lubrication methods for vehicle drive systems. As disclosed by Bodary, it is well known for a vehicle drive system lubricate system to include an elongated tubular conduits that defines a passage. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include an elongated tubular conduits that define a passage as taught by Bodary, as such a modification would provide the ability to direct lubricating oil to specific components of the differential assembly.
Regarding Claim 3, Onishi further discloses;
wherein gravity propels the oil to the portion of the differential assembly from the secondary oil reservoir via the at least one passage. (Fig. 5 and paragraph 40 demonstrates oil returning to the main oil reservoir from the secondary reservoir 18 via the drain hole 16.)
Regarding Claim 4, Onishi does not disclose wherein the at least one passage is configured to convey oil to a bearing of the differential assembly. However, Bodary teaches;
wherein the at least one passage (conduits 52, 54)  is configured to convey oil to a bearing of the differential assembly. (Column 9, lines 11-40 describe the conduits which may deliver oil to input and output shaft bearings.)
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include at least one passage which is configured to convey oil to a bearing of the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to vehicle drive systems. As disclosed by Bodary, it is well known for a vehicle drive system to include at least one passage which is configured to convey oil to a bearing of the differential assembly. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include at least one passage which is configured to convey oil to a bearing of the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as such a modification would provide the ability to direct lubricating oil to specific drive components.
Regarding Claim 5, Bodary teaches;
wherein the bearing is a side bearing. (Column 9, lines 23-40 describe the bearing as an output shaft bearing.)
Regarding Claim 6, Onishi does not disclose first and second passages that are configured to convey oil to  first and second side bearings of the differential assembly. However, Bodary teaches;
wherein the at least one passage comprises:
a first passage (first conduit 52) that is configured to convey oil to a first side bearing of the differential assembly; and
a second passage (second conduit 54) that is configured to convey oil to a second side bearing of the differential assembly opposite the first side bearing.
Bodary describes the oil distribution conduits as supplying oil to the input and output shaft bearings but also states, in Column 10, lines 4-29, that the conduits may supply lubricant, among other components, the differential assembly and the bearings that support it.
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include first and second passages that are configured to convey oil to first and second side bearings of the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to vehicle drive systems. As disclosed by Bodary, it is well known for a vehicle drive system to include first and second passages that are configured to convey oil to first and second side bearings of the differential assembly. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include first and second passages that are configured to convey oil to first and second side bearings of the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as such a modification would provide the ability to direct lubrication to specific drive components. (Column 10, lines 4-29, Bodary).
Regarding Claim 7, Onishi further discloses;
wherein the opening is axially aligned with the ring gear and is oriented to generally face teeth of the ring gear. (Figs. 5 and 8 shows the opening 15 in gasket 10 aligned such that it faces the ring gear teeth. The opening spans the width of the cover and is thereby axially aligned with the ring gear.)

Regarding Claim 8, Onishi does not disclose the opening is axially offset from the ring gear and a portion of the ring gear is positioned radially outboard of a portion of the oil reservoir. However, Bodary teaches;
wherein the opening (inlet 230; Fig. 4, Column 6, lines 56-67, Bodary) is axially offset from the ring gear (ring gear 180; Fig. 3) and a portion of the ring gear is positioned radially outboard of a portion of the secondary oil reservoir with respect to the axis about which the ring gear rotates. (Figs. 3-4 demonstrate the tank has an open top (230) and two side compartments (220,222) in which to collect and hold lubricant. The ring gear extends above the bottom panel (242) of the tank such that it can splash lubricant into the open in the upper portion of the tank. Column 6, lines 56-67, Fig. 3)
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include an opening axially offset from the ring gear where a portion of the ring gear is positioned outboard of a portion of the oil reservoir as taught by Bodary, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to vehicle drive systems. As disclosed by Bodary, it is well known for a vehicle drive system to include an opening axially offset from the ring gear where a portion of the ring gear is positioned outboard of a portion of the oil reservoir. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include an opening axially offset from the ring gear where a portion of the ring gear is positioned outboard of a portion of the oil reservoir as taught by Bodary, as such a modification would provide the ability to provide for the collection of lubricant flung off the ring gear in an auxiliary reservoir thereby reducing drag and churning losses in the differential assembly. (Column 11, lines 14-38, Bodary).
Regarding Claim 10, Onishi discloses;
a differential assembly (differential apparatus 1; Fig. 1) that is operably coupled to a drive source via a ring gear (ring gear 7; Fig. 5); and
a housing (differential carrier 2) that defines a primary oil reservoir (gear accommodation chamber 3) in which the differential assembly is disposed, (see Fig. 5)
a secondary oil reservoir (lubricating oil reservoir 18),
an opening (opening 15) via which the primary oil reservoir and the secondary oil reservoir are in fluid communication, and
at least one passage wherein rotation of the ring gear is configured to deliver oil into the secondary oil reservoir from the primary oil reservoir via the opening, (opening 15 allows oil to be thrown off the ring gear and deposited into the secondary chamber housed in the cover),
the at least one passage is configured to convey oil from the secondary oil reservoir to a portion of the differential assembly. (oil returns to the main chamber via drain holes 16; Fig. 5)
Onishi does not disclose an electric drive unit, a transmission assembly or that the housing body also contains the transmission assembly. However Bodary teaches;
An electric drive unit, comprising: a motor that drives rotation of a rotor shaft; (Column 2, lines 11-25 of Bodary describe the axle assembly as being attached to a torque source such as an electric motor or an internal combustion engine. See also Fig. 2)
a transmission assembly; (Column 3, line 60 to column 5, line 7 describes the drop gear set 26 and clutch collar 28 as transmitting power from input shaft 24 to the differential unit at pinion 32. See also Fig. 2)
coupled with a differential (differential assembly 34)  via a ring gear (ring gear 180; Fig. 2) (Column 5, Lines 8-36 of Bodary describe the differential assembly (34) as receiving torque from the drive pinion (32) via the ring gear (180).)
a housing in which the transmission assembly and differential assembly are disposed, (differential  housing 62, axle housing 60, cover 84; Fig. 2)
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include an electric drive unit comprising a motor that drives rotation of a rotor shaft, a transmission assembly, and a housing which contains the transmission along with the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to vehicle drive systems. As disclosed by Bodary, it is well known for a vehicle drive system to consist of an electric drive comprising a motor that drives a rotor shaft, a transmission assembly, and a housing which contains the transmission along with the differential assembly. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include an electric drive comprising a motor that drives rotation of a rotor shaft, a transmission assembly, and a housing which contains the transmission along with the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as such a modification would provide the ability to utilize an electric motor as a motive power source for a vehicle.
Regarding Claim 11, Onishi does not disclose, at least one elongated tubular conduit, however Bodary teaches;
wherein the at least one passage (conduits 52, 54; Figs. 3, 4, Column 9, lines 11-22) is defined by at least one elongated tubular conduit.
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include an elongated tubular conduits that define a passage as taught by Bodary, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to lubrication methods for vehicle drive systems. As disclosed by Bodary, it is well known for a vehicle drive system lubricate system to include an elongated tubular conduits that defines a passage. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include an elongated tubular conduits that define a passage as taught by Bodary, as such a modification would provide the ability to direct lubricating oil to specific components of the differential assembly.
Regarding Claim 12, Onishi further discloses;
wherein the at least one passage comprises: a first passage that is defined by a first elongated tubular conduit; and a second passage that is defined by a second elongated tubular conduit. (Figs. 3, 4 and paragraph 54 describes the lubrication conduits 52 and 54)
Regarding Claim 13, Onishi does not disclose first and second passages that are configured to convey oil to  first and second side bearings of the differential assembly. However, Bodary teaches;
wherein the first passage (first conduit 52)  conveys oil to a first side bearing of the differential assembly, and the second passage (second conduit 54) conveys oil to a second side bearing of the differential assembly.
Bodary describes the oil distribution conduits as supplying oil to the input and output shaft bearings but also states, in column 10, lines 4-29, that the conduits may supply lubricant, among other components, the differential assembly and the bearings that support it.
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include first and second passages that are configured to convey oil to first and second side bearings of the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to vehicle drive system. As disclosed by Bodary, it is well known for a vehicle drive system to include first and second passages that are configured to convey oil to first and second side bearings of the differential assembly. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include first and second passages that are configured to convey oil to first and second side bearings of the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as such a modification would provide the ability to direct lubrication to specific drive components. (Column 10, lines 4-29, Bodary).
Regarding Claim 14, Bodary further teaches;
wherein the at least one elongated tubular conduit angles vertically downward to an outlet, such that the oil is conveyed within the at least one passage by gravity. (Column 9, lines 23-40 state that the conduits 52, 54 may slope downwards away from the lubricant reservoir to further facilitate the flow of lubricant.)
Regarding Claim 15, Onishi further discloses;
wherein the opening is axially aligned with the ring gear and is oriented to generally face teeth of the ring gear. (Figs. 5 and 8 shows the opening 15 in gasket 10 aligned such that it faces the ring gear teeth. The opening spans the width of the cover and is thereby axially aligned with the ring gear.)
Regarding Claim 16, Onishi does not disclose the opening is axially offset from the ring gear and a portion of the ring gear is positioned radially outboard of a portion of the oil reservoir. However, Bodary teaches;
wherein the opening (inlet 230; Fig. 4, Column 6, lines 56-67, Bodary) is axially offset from the ring gear (ring gear 180; Fig. 3) and a portion of the ring gear is positioned radially outboard of a portion of the secondary oil reservoir with respect to the axis about which the ring gear rotates. (Figs. 3-4 demonstrate the tank has an open top (230) and two side compartments (220,222) in which to collect and hold lubricant. The ring gear extends above the bottom panel (242) of the tank such that it can splash lubricant into the open in the upper portion of the tank. Column 6, lines 56-67, Fig. 3)
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include an opening axially offset from the ring gear where a portion of the ring gear is positioned outboard of a portion of the oil reservoir as taught by Bodary, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to vehicle drive systems. As disclosed by Bodary, it is well known for a vehicle drive system to include an opening axially offset from the ring gear where a portion of the ring gear is positioned outboard of a portion of the oil reservoir. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include an opening axially offset from the ring gear where a portion of the ring gear is positioned outboard of a portion of the oil reservoir as taught by Bodary, as such a modification would provide the ability to provide for the collection of lubricant flung off the ring gear in an auxiliary reservoir thereby reducing drag and churning losses in the differential assembly. (Column 11, lines 14-38, Bodary).
Regarding Claim 17, Onishi discloses;
An assembly, comprising: a gearset (ring gear 7 and pinion gear 8; Fig. 5); and
a housing (differential carrier 2) that defines a primary oil reservoir (gear accommodation chamber 3) in which the gearset is disposed,
a secondary oil reservoir (lubricating reservoir 18), an opening via which the primary oil reservoir and the secondary oil reservoir are in fluid communication (opening 15), and
at least one passage (drain hole 16) that is configured to convey oil from the secondary oil reservoir into the primary oil reservoir during operation of the gearset. (Paragraph 69 describes the flow rate through the hole 16 is determined by the amount of oil scooped up by the ring gear and supplied to oil reservoir 18.)
Onishi does not disclose at least one passage defined by an elongated tubular conduit, however Bodary teaches;
wherein the at least one passage (conduits 52, 54; Figs. 3, 4, Column 9, lines 11-22) defined by an elongated tubular conduit.
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include an elongated tubular conduits that define a passage as taught by Bodary, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to lubrication methods for vehicle drive systems. As disclosed by Bodary, it is well known for a vehicle drive system lubricate system to include an elongated tubular conduits that defines a passage. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include an elongated tubular conduits that define a passage as taught by Bodary, as such a modification would provide the ability to direct lubricating oil to specific components of the differential assembly.
Regarding Claim 18, Onishi further disclose;
wherein the gearset is a portion of a differential assembly. (Paragraph 33 describes the differential device as containing the ring gear 7 and pinion 8)
Regarding Claim 19, Bodary further teaches;
a bearing, wherein the elongated tubular conduit (conduits 52, 54)  defines an outlet of the at least one passage that is proximate to the bearing, such that oil is conveyed to the bearing via the at least one passage. (Column 9, lines 11-40 describe the conduits may delivery oil to input and output shaft bearings.)
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include at least one passage which is configured to convey oil to a bearing of the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to vehicle drive systems. As disclosed by Bodary, it is well known for a vehicle drive system to include at least one passage which is configured to convey oil to a bearing of the differential assembly. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include at least one passage which is configured to convey oil to a bearing of the differential assembly as taught by Bodary, as such a modification would provide the ability to direct lubricating oil to specific drive components.
Regarding Claim 20, Onishi further discloses;
wherein the housing comprises: a housing body (differential carrier 2; Fig. 5) that defines the primary oil reservoir (gear accommodation chamber 3 and lubricant OL; Fig. 5);
a housing cover (cover 4); and
a gasket (gasket 10) that is disposed between the housing cover and the housing body, wherein the gasket and the housing cover cooperate to define the secondary oil reservoir (lubricating sump 18).

Claim 9 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Onishi, in view of Bodary as applied to claim 8 above, and further in view of Okada (US 2012/0295751 A1).
Regarding Claim 9, Onishi in view of Bodary does not disclose a housing cover which includes a plurality of ribs that guide oil delivered onto the housing cover from the ring gear axially toward the opening. However, Okada teaches;
wherein the housing cover includes a plurality of ribs (guide portion 64; Fig. 11, 13) that guide oil delivered onto the housing cover from the ring gear (ring gear 14) axially toward the opening. (Fig. 11 and paragraph 62 describe the purpose of the sides of passageway 67 to direct oil splashed from the ring gear into the lubricant passageway 67.)
A person of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention would have been motivated to modify Onishi to include a housing cover which includes a plurality of ribs that guide oil delivered onto the housing cover from the ring gear axially towards an opening as taught by Okada, as the references and the claimed invention are directed to lubrication methods for vehicle drive systems. As disclosed by Okada, it is well known for a housing cover to include a plurality of ribs that guide oil delivered onto the housing cover from the ring gear axially towards an opening. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Onishi to include a housing cover which includes a plurality of ribs that guide oil delivered onto the housing cover from the ring gear axially towards an opening as taught by Okada, as such a modification would provide the ability to direct splashed oil from the ring gear to desired lubrication points. (Paragraph 64, Okada).
Conclusion
